models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods move as gifts that create duties to give and return, so pay comes through reciprocal exchange and standing rather than a price set in a market. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that obligations to give and return bind people together, so a worker's pay can be a favour that the giver may withdraw, and those without standing have no claim to a fixed sum. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm balances its work against household needs, so the household sets its own output, and work is measured against what the family needs rather than against a wage rate. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so output stops once household needs are met, and any hired help is paid whatever rate the household can afford, with no floor to protect it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects goods and redistributes them to workers and officials, so pay arrives as regular allocations from common stores, with no wage bargain needed to fix it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates surplus, so each worker's share depends on the centre's decisions rather than on any set rate or bargain, and a worker who loses that share has no market to turn to. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that labour is held through ownership, so the cost of labour is fixed in advance rather than set by a wage market, which lets owners plan output and costs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through ownership, so enslaved people receive no wage and no floor, and what they are given is set by the owner, with no contract to enforce. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives land and protection in return for labour services, so a tenant has a secure holding and protection in hard times. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that peasants owe labour services and rents to a lord, so money wages are rare, labour is owed whatever it would earn, and tenants cannot move freely to seek better pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: The case England's Statute of Artificers: wages fixed by local justices reports that pay in urban trades came under guild authority, while farm wages were left to local justices. The account rests on summaries, not the statute's text, and research on enforcement is divided, so no verdict is given.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry and set statutes, so pay in a closed trade is set by the masters, and newcomers wait outside it with no route to better pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates trade toward a surplus, so employers in export trades get predictable labour costs under state rules, and employment in those trades is backed by policy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case England's Statute of Artificers: wages fixed by local justices reports that justices fixed rates each year, subject to central approval, and that farm wages were left to them. The account rests on summaries, not the statute's text. Summaries describe a cap on wages among its aims, not verified here; if so, the act set a ceiling, not a legal minimum. Pay fixed from above, and possibly capped, is the worst practice here. Source: University of Exeter labour-history web page (year not given); D. M. Woodward, The Local Historian (1969); R. Keith Kelsall, Wage Regulation under the Statute of Artificers (1938)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that only the land yields a net product and grain trade should be free, so farm pay follows what the land yields and food prices follow supply. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, so artisans and other workers outside farming are counted as unproductive, and pay in those trades gets no state floor and is left to the market. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: The case New Jersey's 1992 minimum wage rise and fast-food jobs reports a 1994 study, in one comparison region, that found no sign of job cuts, and a 2000 critique by Neumark and Wascher that argued different data show job losses. The sources, which summarise the study, give no verdict on the dispute, so pay set by competition with no legal floor is best only if the critique holds.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out, so pay is left to bargaining between each worker and each employer, and low-paid workers have no floor if they lack other offers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so wage rates signal where labour is scarce, workers move to where pay is highest, and no planner sets them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, so pay in a boom fuelled by cheap credit is set by borrowed demand and can fall sharply when credit tightens and jobs are lost. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: The case New Jersey's 1992 minimum wage rise and fast-food jobs reports that a 2000 critique by Neumark and Wascher argued that different data show job losses, while a 1994 study, in one comparison region, found no sign of job cuts. The sources, which summarise the study, give no verdict, so pay left to markets, with no legal floor, is best if the critique is right.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that steady money, deregulation and privatisation leave pay to markets, so workers with little bargaining power can face low pay with no floor and no public body to check it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Friedman, Capitalism and Freedom; Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps, so demand and jobs are kept up when the economy turns down, and pay is less likely to fall sharply. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending falls in booms, so public pay and wage support can be held down in strong years, leaving workers to bear the swing of the cycle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: The case Germany's 2015 minimum wage and employment reports that several studies of a legal minimum of 8.50 euros an hour find mostly small to moderate effects. The sources are abstracts and snippets, not full studies, and the studies use different data, so their figures are not directly comparable.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so where few employers hire in a town they may hold pay down unless that order checks them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle

models.best: The case Saltsjöbaden Agreement: pay bargained by unions and employers reports that unions and employers bargained pay and conditions with each other, with the government largely on the sidelines, through a joint council and grievance procedures. The sources differ on its scope, and none describes a statutory minimum wage.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that national bargaining sets terms for whole sectors, so workers outside the bargain, or new to it, get terms they had no part in setting. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries and disciplines firms by performance, so pay in favoured export firms can track output, and state support is tied to measured results. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks the favoured industries, so pay in other sectors lags, and workers there have no floor and little say in how pay is set. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle; Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land rather than labour is taxed, so wages carry no tax of this kind, and the rent of land funds public services. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land values carry public funding, so public pay and services rise and fall with land prices, and a downturn in land values can cut budgets for the workers who run them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities replace wage competition, so members share work and its product in common rather than selling their labour to the highest bidder. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example, so pay depends on founders' vision and small funds, and workers outside the communities have no floor to protect them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit lent at cost and free contracts let workers keep the full value of their work, so pay is the whole product of labour rather than a share taken by rent. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts set terms, so a worker without a mutual to join may accept whatever pay is offered, with no floor to stop it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own the firm and share the surplus between users and workers, so pay rises with results and workers have a voice in how the surplus is divided. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members own and share the surplus, so a small or closed membership may run the firm for insiders and leave newcomers out, paid less or not at all. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that there are no wages and goods are shared according to need within federated communes, so pay is replaced by common provision, and no worker's share depends on a contract. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no contract, so no body can set or enforce a floor, and any fair share of work depends on the goodwill of the commune. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, so pay and conditions in each trade are set by the workers who do the work, not by a state. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes are the main weapon, so long stoppages cost workers their pay for the duration, and a general strike can halt pay for everyone. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: The case Trade Boards Act: binding minimum pay in sweated trades reports that trade boards set minimum pay rates that became binding in low-paid sweated trades, for men and women alike and for home workers as well as factory workers. It covers the 1909 Act only, and both sources are undated; the book's text was not read.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that reform is gradual and public enterprise is run by officials, so pay floors reach trades one stage at a time, and low-paid workers wait for each stage. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fabian Essays in Socialism; Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through guild-like councils, so pay is settled in councils where workers have a voice, alongside the state as one partner. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that several councils share control, so no single body sets pay, and disputes among staff, councils and the state can stall pay settlements for long periods. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: The case Soviet industrial wage structure: stated reform goals reports that a 1977 paper described the goals as a more consistent basic wage structure and equal pay for equal work, with consolidated scales and base rates pulled closer together. The paper gives stated goals, not outcomes, and says nothing about later decades.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output, prices and investment, so pay scales are fixed from above and cannot easily track local shortages, skills or workers' own choices. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System; First Five-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices, so an enterprise's pay bill can respond to what it sells, within rules that a central board sets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, so the rules for pay are decided above the enterprise, and workers have little say over terms the board fixes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that, once classes disappear, distribution follows need, so the wage bargain gives way to common provision according to what each person needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state comes first and withers away later, so during the transition the state sets pay, and the timing of the change is left open. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors sits alongside markets under party direction, so pay floors can be set to suit local conditions and reform can be phased in step by step. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case China's provincial minimum wage rules from 2004 reports that a paper by Fang and Lin links minimum wage increases to job losses in eastern and central China, falling on women, young adults and low-skilled workers. That finding comes from one conference paper, and the sources are secondary commentary that does not confirm the rules still apply. Source: Commission analysis, 'Most Provincial-Level Governments Issue Hourly Minimum Wage Standards' (year not given); Fang and Lin, IZA conference paper (2014)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, so pay is set by councils, with jobs balanced in complexity, and neither markets nor central planners set it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils reach decisions through repeated proposals, so pay settlements can be slow, and workers who lack time for repeated rounds of meetings may have less say over their own pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into corporations, so pay and job terms are settled within one framework for each trade, rather than through rival bargains. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case Trustees of Labour in Nazi Germany set pay scales reports that a 1933 US dispatch, passing on the Labour Minister's view, said state-appointed trustees would set pay scales until a corporatist reorganisation was complete. Cambridge University Press material calls them state functionaries with authority over pay and job terms, but the dispatch gives a stated plan, not the trustees' decisions, and the Cambridge item gives no wage rules. Source: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1933, volume II, document 188 (US government document series); Cambridge University Press book page on the Nazi economy (year not given)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, so pay can be linked to the results of a shared venture, and zakat redistributes wealth to those in need. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and trust underpins contracts, so workers rely on the good faith of employers rather than enforceable minimum terms, and pay disputes can rest on trust alone. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so pay is judged by whether it supports a modest but sufficient life, and small local firms keep workers close to the people who employ them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that consumption is moderate and production small-scale, so pay may be set for modest needs alone, with no formal standard for workers in larger or distant enterprises to appeal to. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a just wage lets a worker build property and support a family, so pay is set to meet that aim, and subsidiarity keeps pay decisions with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small enterprise is widespread, so a small employer with few alternatives may pay what the local trade allows, and no national floor is set to protect workers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a social floor lies under everyone within planetary limits, so a legal floor on pay protects low earners without relying on growth to lift them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so real pay gains that depend on rising output may be limited, and workers in shrinking sectors could face pay cuts. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so a worker can refuse poor terms and keep a secure income, and pay need not carry the whole cost of subsistence. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is paid regardless of earnings, so employers may hold pay down knowing the state covers basic needs, and the cost of low pay shifts onto taxpayers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government issuing its own currency can fund full employment, so a shortage of finance need not keep willing workers out of paid work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so pay floors set above what output can support could push prices up and erode the real value of wages. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities design, monitor and enforce their own rules for a shared resource, so the people who share a resource set and check its shares of work and income themselves. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that rules must be monitored and enforced by the community itself, so a small or divided group may fail to enforce its share rules, leaving some members underpaid. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: A legal minimum wage in low-paid trades, set by a public council of unions, employers and independent members, with pay bargained above it by sector. The floor is a minimum, never a cap, and each rise is tested for its effect on jobs before it is made permanent.
compromise.details: Keeps: a legal floor set by trade boards, from Fabian socialism and the case Trade Boards Act: binding minimum pay in sweated trades; joint pay bargaining, from Nordic social democracy and the case Saltsjöbaden Agreement: pay bargained by unions and employers; small to moderate effects (abstracts and snippets), from Social market economy and the case Germany's 2015 minimum wage and employment. Blocks: pay fixed from above and possibly capped, from Mercantilism, with a floor that is never a cap; job losses among the least skilled, from Chinese market socialism (one conference paper), with a jobs test before each rise. Test: hourly pay at the bottom, and jobs in affected trades, against similar areas, for several years after each change. Source: University of Warwick digitised collection on the Trade Boards (year not given); University of Alberta business school page on the 1938 basic agreement (year not given); University of Exeter labour-history web page (year not given); IAB, Bossler and Gerner (2016); Fang and Lin, IZA conference paper (2014)
